newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Europe, without policy, lurches towards action.
newsitem.headline: Europe, without policy, lurches towards action.

text.p: European states lurched towards some form of humanitarian intervention in central Africa on Monday, but critics immediately charged they were devoid of any overall policy likely to prevent a repeat of past errors.

France, taking the lead as so often in African crises, proposed urgent talks with the United States, its European partners, and Africa on an action plan to restore security in the area and help avert disaster for up to one million refugees.

Foreign Minister Herve de Charette indicated a possible international operation would be temporary and would allow up to one million mainly Hutu refugees to return to their camps and villagers to return home.

But aid workers and regional experts said there were no signs any European capitals were prepared to try and tackle the region's complex patchwork of tribal, economic and political crises which lie at the heart of the current instability.

"They are talking about putting food in people's mouths again, but that is not enough. That is exactly what created this mess in the first place," said the head of one humanitarian organisation, who asked not to be named.

Huge camps in eastern Zaire teeming with Hutu refugees, who fled the Tutsi victory which ended Rwanda's 1994 Hutu-inspired genocide, became military bases for rebels aiming to overthrow Tutsi-led governments in Rwanda and Burundi.
Many of the leaders of the genocide of some one million people, mainly Tutsis, moved freely around the camps and ordered their followers not to respond to calls to return home.
"Unless people learn the lesson of last time, and are prepared to disarm thugs, then we will just recreate the conditions which led to this current insecurity," the aid official added.

Regional experts say Zaire's minority Banyamulenge Tutsis have received support from Rwanda's guerrilla-hardened army, which fought its way to power in a four-year bush war, and have now virtually succeeded in creating a "buffer zone".

The rebels, officially involved in a separate conflict with the Zairean authorities, offered a temporary ceasefire on Monday in the town of Bukavu, one of a string they now hold along the borders with Rwanda and Burundi.

With memories of the failed peace mission in Somalia still present in a United States dominated by presidential election issues, Washington will not endorse an African adventure, diplomats and analysts say.
Paris, which launched Operation Turquoise at the height of Rwanda's 1994 genocide, is ready to act, but only if asked to do so by the international community.
"They want some form of U.N., European, or regional cover. They will not go it alone," said one EU defence ministry source.
Italy has said it would support such an action while Belgium, the former colonial power in the region, has called a meeting of EU ministers for Thursday.
Brussels says it will support an international relief operation, likely to focus on seizing key airports and opening relief corridors to stranded refugees, but is admanant it will not send troops.

Belgium lost 10 paratroopers, then serving with a U.N. force, when the genocide started in Rwanda in 1994 following suspicions the country had connived in the assassination of then-President Juvenal Habyarimana.

A British Foreign Office statement said any intervention force would have to be immediately effective in solving problems on the ground and would have to operate under the auspices of the United Nations.

The U.N. refugee agency chief urgently appealed on Monday for a ceasefire in eastern Zaire and called for the creation of internationally protected humanitarian corridors to coax thousands of Rwandan refugees into Rwanda.
Sadako Ogata, the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees, told Reuters that she foresaw the establishment of a corridor from east Zaire's Goma town into Rwanda.
"I'd like to have heavy international presence in order to give a sense of confidence to the refugees who are very frightened," she said.
